parts.text:
From abroad, this created an image of Denmark as a country where people were unusually free to live differently.

‘A porn

’

In 1969, when the Danish parliament legalised pornographic images , its decision was highly controversial among Danes. But it attracted considerable attention internationally, particularly in West Germany, where the new government under Chancellor Willy Brandt prepared a similar reform.

The result was not simply a change in Danish law. People, products and money began moving across the

.

Government officials travelled to Copenhagen to learn about the effects of the liberalisation. West Germans travelled to Denmark to buy pornography. Danish

gained access to a much larger market south of the border. Denmark could even be imagined in West Germany as a kind of porn paradise.

Our research into West German reactions to Denmark’s liberalisation between 1965 and 1985 shows how the country became

with a new kind of sexual freedom.

Danish homosexual people and activists also developed connections with larger gay communities in West Germany, particularly in Berlin and Hamburg. And Denmark developed its own naturist culture, not least inspired by the German movement of freikörperkultur (

FRY-kur-per-kul-toor) or “free body culture”. People gathered to swim, sunbathe and socialise naked.

People, ideas and practices were therefore moving in both directions across the border.

Reputation and national values

Over time, these developments helped turn Denmark’s reputation for social

into something more than an international image. It became part of how Denmark could describe itself.

In 2016, for example, the Danish government asked the public to identify values considered particularly important to Danish society. The resulting Danmarkskanon, or Danish Canon, included ten such values. One was frisind (pronounced free-sin) – a word that can mean

, tolerance or freedom from conventional moral constraints.

The Canon described frisind in terms of openness

traditional moral ideas, the body and sexuality. It pointed to Denmark’s relaxed attitude towards nudity, tolerance of different forms of family and sexual life, alternative lifestyles and the legalisation of pornography.

By this point, what had once been a contested and internationally

reputation had become something that could be presented as part of Denmark’s cultural heritage. But that does not necessarily mean Danes have always been uniquely tolerant.

The Danish criminologist Berl Kutchinsky (1935-1995) studied the liberalisation of pornography
and he was sceptical of precisely this idea. He argued that Denmark’s exceptional liberalism was something of a myth.

reading.title: 主旨、理解与信息定位
reading.instruction: 阅读原文后回答 5 道选择题：1 道主旨、1 道内容理解、1 道段落细节、2 道信息定位。段落细节题以题干指定段落为准。

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarises the overall focus of this article?
options: Denmark's reputation for open-mindedness has a more complicated history than stereotypes suggest.
A public poetry project connects Shakespeare's influence with everyday journeys on the Underground.
The discovery of a Roman fort revives interest in an emperor's place in Welsh tradition.
Tove Jansson's Hobbit illustrations express an imaginative understanding of childhood.
questions.explanation: 把标题与全文各段的中心内容连起来判断主旨，避免把同一主题下的其他话题当成本文重点。
questions.evidence: But its history suggests something more complicated: Denmark’s reputation for open-mindedness was, at least partly, made through its relationships with other countries.

questions.prompt: Which audience helped shape Denmark's liberal reputation from the 1960s?
questions.explanation: 第 5 段提供了作答依据。正确选项用不同说法表达了文中的信息；请比较范围、数量、因果关系与限定词。
questions.evidence: From the 1960s onwards, West Germany became an important audience for Denmark’s emerging reputation as a more liberal society.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is explicitly made in paragraph 13?
options: And Danish activists have helped push ideas about sexuality and family life in new directions.
In 1969, when the Danish parliament legalised pornographic images , its decision was highly controversial among Danes.
You can see it in the country’s history: Denmark was the first country in the world to legalise pornography.
Our research into West German reactions to Denmark’s liberalisation between 1965 and 1985 shows how the country became associated with a new kind of sexual freedom.

questions.evidence: In 1969, when the Danish parliament legalised pornographic images , its decision was highly controversial among Danes.
